title: Theming & Brand
text:
Note



Skip this page unless you’re re-theming. If you’re just writing poster content on the templates as shipped, you don’t need to know Bootstrap (Bootstrap contributors, n.d.) or SCSS (Sass, n.d.) at all — the colors and fonts are already set up. Come back here only if you’re forking for a different organization’s palette, or troubleshooting a contrast/color regression.

title: Theming & Brand
text:
1 Re-coloring the templates
If you fork this repo for another organization, the palette lives in a small number of places. The check-contrast.R exists so you can prove your new colors are still accessible against WCAG (Initiative (WAI), n.d.) rather than assume it:

scss/poster-common.scss: the $au-* tokens under scss:defaults drive the whole web version.
_brand.yml: the same palette for Quarto’s brand-aware theming. Keep the two in sync; some Bootstrap variables come from here rather than from the stylesheet.
Print footers are per template: footer-color and footer-text-color in each poster.qmd YAML.

Then re-run the audit:
Rscript scripts/check-contrast.R                 # fails below WCAG AA
Rscript scripts/check-contrast.R --require-aaa   # fails below AAA
It parses your new hex values out of the stylesheet and each template’s YAML and re-measures every pair, so the check follows your colors instead of the ones committed here. render-all.R runs it as part of the full suite.
Some technical considerations to ensure proper contrast, all covered by the script:

The banner is a gradient. Text has to clear the threshold against the lighter stop, not just the dark one.

Auditing only the dark stop can cause issues.
The script reads both stops out of the linear-gradient() declaration and checks each separately.

The gradient’s light stop is capped by its text, not by taste. White normal-size text needs 7:1 for AAA, which puts a hard ceiling on how light $au-blue-banner can be; hence a dedicated token rather than reusing $au-blue.

Note the label originally used a dimmed tint, and a tinted label is still normal-size text, so AAA would have demanded 7:1 of the tint and forced the light stop nearly to navy, flattening the gradient.
The labels are plain white instead and read as secondary through case, tracking, and weight, which keeps about half the gradient’s luminance range.

Opacity silently undoes contrast. Quarto’s own stylesheet sets opacity: .8 on .quarto-title-meta-heading.

Left in place, white at 80% over the light stop composites to roughly #d6dee7 and measures 5.31:1 which is AA, not the 7.21:1 the color alone suggests.
poster-common.scss overrides it back to opacity: 1; if you introduce translucency anywhere, remember the audit reads declared colors, not composited ones.

Accent colors and text colors are held to different bars. WCAG asks 3:1 of large text and graphics, but 4.5:1 (AA) or 7:1 (AAA) of normal-size text.

$au-blue is perfectly fine as a banner and border color yet was not fine as link text, which is why $au-blue-text exists as a separate darker token so links can darken without darkening the banner.
Size is the other lever, and the script reads each rule’s declared font-size rather than taking anyone’s word for it: a heading at 24px or more (1.5rem at the default root size) is audited as large text automatically, which is how 02’s red headings reach AAA without touching the red.
Shrink such a heading back below 24px and the audit silently re-classifies it as normal text and the stricter bar returns.

Inline code inherits the brand grey. Bootstrap derives --bs-code-color from it, so $au-grey sets both the acknowledgments/references block and every `inline code` span.

These templates use a lot of inline code, so that pair is audited explicitly.

Rule colors are parsed, not restated. The script reads the color: and background: declarations straight out of the four stylesheets (resolving palette variables and gradient stops), so editing a rule such as the ethics panel’s cream background is picked up automatically.

Its source column shows where each value came from. The exceptions are Bootstrap-derived variables (--bs-body-color, --bs-code-color, $link-color), which no rule states; those resolve from the palette instead.

Renaming a class breaks the audit loudly. A lookup that finds no matching selector or property is a hard error naming the failed selector, not a silently skipped row, so the audit cannot quietly stop covering something you renamed.
A rule that matches nothing gets no row. .ethics-panel h2, .ethics-panel h3 is defensive styling with no counterpart in the rendered HTML: the panel’s leads are **bold** (so <strong>, not a heading), and the section’s own h2 is a sibling of the panel div rather than a descendant.

Auditing it would have reported a contrast figure for text that never appears. If you do put a heading inside the panel, add the row.


Current status: all 22 audited pairs reach AAA.

The last AA-only pair was 02-modern-cards’s red section headings on white (6.28:1 against a 7:1 bar).
Raising them from 1.1rem to 1.5rem makes them “large text”, where the bar is 4.5:1, which was preferable to darkening the brand red.
Because every pair now clears AAA, --require-aaa is a usable gate rather than an aspiration so CI runs it that way.

title: Theming & Brand
text:
2 _brand.yml and your workflow
As flagged on the Home page, Quarto’s brand theming is still evolving. This section describes how _brand.yml fits into these templates today; see Quarto’s own Brand guide (Posit Software, PBC, n.d.) for the full, current spec.
What it’s for here:

_brand.yml is the single source of the AU color palette and typography.
Quarto’s brand-aware HTML theming reads it automatically, you don’t include or reference it from any .qmd, Quarto just picks it up from the project root.

What it actually reaches:

In practice, only the web (html) output consumes it directly for color, via Bootstrap variables Quarto derives from the brand palette, e.g., --bs-body-color, --bs-code-color, --bs-link-color.

See the “Bootstrap var” rows above.

The print (poster-typst) output does not read _brand.yml’s color palette at all.

Print colors come from each template’s own YAML (footer-color, footer-text-color) and from raw Typst blocks, so a color change needs to be made in both places.
See step 5 of Fork this repo and build your poster.


Typography is the mirror image of color, and worth calling out on its own.

_brand.yml declares Source Sans 3 and STIX Two Text as typography.fonts resources (source: google).
For print, this is confirmed working: poster.typ hardcodes STIX Two Text for the body, Quarto injects a Source Sans 3 show rule for headings, and Quarto fetches both from Google into .quarto/typst/fonts/ at render time, verified by the absence of Typst’s unknown font family warning, which is a hard compiler signal, not a guess.
For web, this is also confirmed working.

An earlier approach grepped the raw rendered HTML for literal strings like @font-face, but every poster.qmd sets embed-resources: true, which makes Quarto inline its CSS as percent-encoded data:text/css,... URIs rather than plain <style> text, so @font-face appears in the file as %40font%2Dface and a literal-string search never finds it.

Decoding those URIs (rather than grepping around them) now shows the rendered HTML for each template does contain a self-hosted @font-face for Source Sans 3 (base64-embedded font data, not a hotlink) and --bs-body-font-family: Source Sans 3 in the compiled Bootstrap variables and font-family:Source Sans 3 on the compiled heading rules, i.e., both the base and headings roles reach the browser correctly.

STIX Two Text is fetched and embedded too, but is never applied to anything on the web side, and correctly so, since _brand.yml’s own comment notes it’s declared only so Typst can find it for print; nothing under base/headings names it for html.
scripts/render-all.R now has a check_fonts() step that decodes each rendered poster.html this way and asserts the @font-face block and --bs-body-font-family variable are both present, so a future regression, or another naive grep, fails loudly instead of silently reading as “not delivered.”

See AGENTS.md’s “Fonts” section for the full before/after and for how the standalone minimal-reproduction project (no custom theme or scss) was re-run with the same decode-first approach and shows the identical, working pattern.

Why it’s kept in sync with the stylesheet by hand, not generated from it:

scss/poster-common.scss (Sass (Sass, n.d.)) defines the same $au-* tokens under scss:defaults for rules Bootstrap’s brand integration doesn’t cover (the banner gradient, the ethics panel, section-card styling).

Nothing currently generates one file from the other, so Re-coloring the templates treats both as required edits, and check-contrast.R reads both.


The logo: key is intentionally left unset because each template places the organization logo explicitly instead. See Shared resources to avoid Quarto rendering a second, automatic brand logo alongside it.
If you fork this for another organization:

Update _brand.yml’s palette and typography alongside scss/poster-common.scss and each template’s footer colors.
Then, re-run Rscript scripts/check-contrast.R --require-aaa to confirm the new combination is still accessible.

title: Templates
text:
The three templates offer different design approaches that may be tailored for a particular purpose.

All three share the same content structure (level-2 ## headings become poster sections/panels automatically) so switching between them is mostly a matter of swapping the YAML/SCSS, not rewriting your text.


templates/01-classic-academic/: traditional 3-column layout (Intro / Methods / Data / Results / Conclusions), serif headings, the closest analog to the old posterdown betterland template.

Print size 42x28 in, 3 Typst columns.




01-classic-academic poster preview


templates/02-modern-cards/: dashboard-style card grid with a bold accent color, headlining its key finding as one sentence rather than an isolated number.

Print size 48x36 in, 2 Typst columns (fewer, larger panels).
This size doubles as a standard conference board size – see Choosing a print size below.
This template’s content was originally short enough that Typst never started the second column at all (everything landed in column 1, leaving column 2 blank except the floated Ethics panel). Fixed by adding a manual #colbreak() (raw Typst, right before ## Evidence) so the figure/table/“What’s Next” content explicitly starts column 2, plus enough added text/a correlation table to make the two columns’ content roughly comparable to 01-classic-academic’s.
The figure itself was always full column width – if you add your own full-page figures, note that out-width: "100%" measured against the page width rather than the current column’s width immediately after a #colbreak() in local testing, overflowing past the margin; setting an explicit absolute out-width (e.g. "20in") sidesteps it.
The Headline Finding is plain markdown, not a per-format .stat block. An earlier draft set the two slope numbers on their own line at 72pt (with duplicated ```{=html}/```{=typst} blocks, since a web-only .stat CSS class doesn’t reach the print output) – bare digits and an arrow glyph with no verb tying them into a sentence, and the arrow’s stroke weight didn’t reliably match the surrounding bold text in either format. It now reads as one sentence (“pooling every species together gives X, but adding species … reverses it to Y”) at body size, so pandoc’s normal **bold** emphasis handles both outputs identically – no raw blocks, no per-format duplication, no font-fallback weight mismatch to chase.




02-modern-cards poster preview


templates/03-minimal-story/: a single flowing narrative column, meant to be read like a short article; flat design, generous whitespace.

Print size 24x52 in (portrait banner), 1 Typst column.




03-minimal-story poster preview



Each preview above (images/previews/preview-*.png) is a 1200px-wide PNG rendered from that template’s own poster-typst PDF. Neither these nor comparison.png below are produced by quarto render; regenerate both with Rscript scripts/make-previews.R after a content change (render the PDFs first).
All three are currently filled in with the same worked example (a Simpson’s-paradox (“Simpson’s Paradox” 2026) analysis of bill shape across penguin species, using palmerpenguins (Horst et al. 2020)) so the three visual styles are directly comparable:



Comparison of the three print posters, one per row



comparison.png stacks the three posters as separate full-width rows (labeled with the template name/size) using the R magick package.

Rows, not side-by-side columns: 03-minimal-story is a tall 24x52in portrait banner, while the other two are landscape (42x28in, 48x36in); scaling all three to a common height for a side-by-side layout shrinks the banner to an unreadable sliver, so each poster instead gets its own row at a common width, sized for legibility.
Each page is rasterized at 2x its target pixel width and downsampled, rather than rendered at full 300 dpi print resolution first – a 48x36in page at 300 dpi is a 14400x10800 bitmap, and the supersampled version is indistinguishable at display sizes here for a fraction of the memory.
03-minimal-story’s header grid (logo/title column widths) defaults to values sized for wider posters, so its long title overflowed the page margin at the default title-font-size. Fixed by setting univ-logo-column-size: 3, title-column-size: 16, title-font-size: 44, and authors-font-size: 28 in that template’s YAML (its 24in width leaves only 20in inside the page’s 2in margins, vs. the extension’s 10in + 20in defaults).


A lesson from filling in the templates: the single-column minimal-story layout has noticeably less capacity per page than the 2- or 3-column layouts. With this same content, it initially overflowed onto a second Typst page at 24x36in;

The version here (with a per-species correlation table and a “What’s Next” section added, to use the extra room well rather than leave it blank) needs 24x52in to stay on one page.
If you adapt this template with less content than that, you can size it down; budget less text per page than you would for the classic or modern-cards versions either way.

title: Templates
text:
2 Choosing a print size
size: (under poster-typst: in each template’s YAML) takes any Typst-compatible "WIDTHxHEIGHT" in inches; it isn’t tied to a specific venue. General poster-session guidance like (Poster Session Guidelines, n.d.) is a useful sanity check on physical constraints (board size, viewing distance) beyond just the numbers below, and a venue’s own call for posters, e.g. (Call for Posters and Demos ACM SIGCOMM 2026, n.d.), is the authoritative source for its board dimensions if it isn’t one of the four below.

A few sizes recur often enough at ML/data-science conferences that it’s worth calling out how the templates map onto them (all landscape, given as the venue’s own H x W convention next to the equivalent size: string):




Venue / convention
H x W
size: string




3ft x 4ft (a common poster-board default)
36in x 48in
"48x36"


ICML
36in x 48in (91cm x 121cm)
"48x36"


NeurIPS (narrower boards)
36in x 60in
"60x36"


NeurIPS (wider boards)
36in x 72in
"72x36"



02-modern-cards already ships at "48x36", so it’s ready for either the generic 3ft x 4ft board size or ICML as-is.

To target a different size (e.g. NeurIPS), on any template:


Change size: to the size: string from the table (or any other "WxH" you need).
If the aspect ratio changes a lot (e.g. going from 48x36 to 72x36), reconsider `num-columns. Wider boards generally read better with one more column than a narrower version of the same layout.
Re-render (quarto render poster.qmd --to poster-typst) and check for overflow onto a second page or, conversely, excess blank space;


Adjust body-font-size, trim/add content, or nudge size: again as needed.
01-classic-academic and 03-minimal-story aren’t currently tuned to any of the sizes above, so budget an iteration or two if you retarget them.

title: Content Guide
text:
Each template includes an “Ethics & Broader Impact” section, placed directly after the methodology section (Approach / How We Studied It / What We Did), covering the three disclosures increasingly expected at AI/data-science venues:

Generative AI use: which tool was used, for what (code scaffolding, prose editing, citation formatting), and a statement that the human author(s) remain fully accountable and that GenAI was not used to fabricate or alter the underlying data — in the spirit of authorship-accountability policies like (ACM Policy on Authorship, n.d.), which hold named authors responsible for a work’s content regardless of what tools assisted in producing it.
Privacy & data governance: whether the data contain PII, whether IRB/GDPR/EU AI Act provisions apply, and under what approvals the source data were collected.
Bias, fairness & broader impact: whether a fairness audit or dual-use/weaponization risk assessment applies, and the computational/environmental cost of the analysis.

The included text is accurate for this demo (public, non-human palmerpenguins (Horst et al. 2020) biometric data; a simple linear regression, not a deployed model).

Treat it as a worked example of the kind of specific, honest statement expected, not boilerplate to copy verbatim.
Rewrite each statement for your own project’s actual data, models, and tool use.

The panel is implemented once per format so it renders correctly in both:

HTML: a ::: {.ethics-panel} ::: div (defined in poster-common.scss); a shaded box with a colored border and ~1.35rem text, larger than surrounding body text for readability.
Print (Typst): a raw ```{=typst} block using #block(..., breakable: false) for the same shaded/bordered look at 20-24pt.
breakable: false is required. Without it, Typst can split the block awkwardly across a column break.

Both copies are wrapped in ::: {.content-visible when-format="..."} so only one appears in each output; if you edit the disclosure text, update both copies.
Acknowledgments are now a plain, uncited sentence for funding and mentorship credit,

This work was performed under the guidance of Dr. Jane A. Smith, Department of Mathematics and Statistics, American University, and was supported by the American University Blair Jones Mathematical Endowment, Grant No. BJME-2026-014.

Each template also has a placeholder Code & data line near Acknowledgments with a GitHub URL to replace with your own repository.
References, Data/software citations appear here automatically when they’re cited in-text with [@key] earlier in the poster. A ready-to-edit example is included in each template.

section: 2 Sizing your own images for print
text:
2 Sizing your own images for print
If you add your own raster image (a photo, screenshot, or diagram exported from other software) to a poster, the pixel dimensions that look fine on a laptop screen or in a slide deck are usually not enough for a multi-foot-wide print.

The same file gets stretched over far more physical inches on paper than on a webpage, so its effective resolution (pixels per inch, once placed) drops accordingly.

The rule of thumb: decide how wide the image will print (in inches), pick a target resolution, and multiply:
\[\text{pixel width needed} = \text{printed width (in)} \times \text{target dpi}\]

150 dpi is a reasonable floor for a poster read from a few feet away.
300 dpi (standard for close-up print/photography) is safer if the image includes fine detail or might be viewed up close.

For reference, images/au-logo-hires.png (the shipped institution logo) is 1327x1361px, which is why it renders sharp at every template’s header size (measured at 490-740 effective dpi depending on the template). This applies to R-generated figures too, not just images you place by hand.

Every template sets fig-format: png (see Notes / gotchas for why), and knitr’s default figure resolution is 96 dpi regardless of the physical print size the figure gets stretched to.

The web version doesn’t have this problem to the same degree.

Browsers display images at whatever pixel density the screen provides (and gracefully downscale an oversized image), so an image sized for print looks fine on the web version too. — The risk only runs one direction: an image sized for the web is usually too low-resolution for print.

title: Quarto Conference Posters
text:
1 The Templates
There are three templates; each a single .qmd file that renders to two outputs:



Format
Purpose
Engine




poster-typst
Large-format print PDF (e.g. 36x24 in)
Typst, via the quarto-ext/typst-templates/poster extension


html
Responsive, scrollable “web poster” for posting online
Quarto HTML + custom SCSS




Because both formats are declared in one format: block, quarto render poster.qmd builds both versions from the same content in one pass.

Run quarto render poster.qmd --to poster-typst or --to html to build just one.

The print PDF is typeset by Typst, not LaTeX. That choice drives several things in these templates (raw ```{=typst} blocks, arbitrary page sizes, no TeX install).

See Why Typst instead of LaTeX? for the reasoning and the trade-offs.

Rscript scripts/render-all.R renders all three templates and then checks the output for known regressions. See Scripts & CI.







NoteIs authoring one poster for two formats worth it?



Worth asking honestly before you invest time customizing both: why not just post the print PDF online and call it your web version?

A conference poster PDF, viewed unzoomed in a browser or on a phone, is usually a wall of text far too small to read without pinching and scrolling panel by panel, the print layout being designed for a person standing a few feet from a physical board, not a screen at arm’s length. Posting it as-is online is easy but often not actually readable there.
A real HTML version, by contrast, reflows to the screen it’s on, is searchable, is accessible to a screen reader, and can be linked from a CV, conference site, or social post without asking the visitor to download or zoom a PDF.

That readability is the actual payoff of this repo’s two-format approach, and it does cost something concrete, documented throughout this site:

Content that can’t be expressed as plain Markdown (the Ethics panel, the headline stat in 02-modern-cards) has to be written twice, once as a raw ```{=html} block and once as ```{=typst}, and kept in sync by hand — see Why Typst instead of LaTeX? and Notes / gotchas.
Layout bugs are per-format and don’t always transfer: the out-width: "100%" overflow in 02-modern-cards and the fig-dpi sharpness issue described in Sizing your own images for print only showed up in the print render; the web version looked correct the whole time (and vice versa for some contrast issues).
Most of scripts/ (column-balance, contrast, font, and structural checks) exists because dual-format authoring makes a regression in one output invisible while looking at the other, e.g., a raw HTML <hr> silently deleting content only from the Typst side (see Notes / gotchas) is the sharpest example.

Our take: it’s worth it if the poster needs to double as a legible, standalone webpage, something you’d actually want a stranger to read on their phone, not just a proof you presented it. If all you need online is an archival record of a physical poster, a shrunk print PDF (or a flattened image of it) is simpler and this repo’s dual-format machinery is more than you need; a single poster-typst render is enough.

section: 3 Fork this repo and build your poster
text:
3 Fork this repo and build your poster
Check the environment requirements below. Then, assuming you’ve forked or cloned this repo to build a poster of your own:

Pick a starting template. Skim the three options in Templates and pick whichever layout fits your content. Each is a self-contained templates/<name>/ folder that renders independently.
Copy the folder, e.g. cp -r templates/01-classic-academic templates/my-poster. Keep it under templates/ so the shared registry in scripts/templates.R, and everything that reads it (render-all.R, check-contrast.R, make-previews.R), picks it up automatically. If your fork will only ever hold one poster, you can instead move that single .qmd (and its sibling .scss) to the project’s top level and delete templates/ entirely; the scripts auto-detect either layout (see Scripts & CI).
Edit the YAML (About - YAML Ain’t Markup Language, n.d.) front matter: title, authors/affiliations, poster-authors, departments, footer contact info, and a print size (any Typst "WIDTHxHEIGHT" in inches. See Choosing a print size for sizes that match common conference boards).
Replace the ## sections with your own content. Each level-2 heading becomes a poster panel automatically, in both outputs. Cite sources with [@bibkey] and add the matching entry to references.bib.
Re-color it if you’re forking for a different organization. The palette lives in a small, documented set of places.

See Re-coloring the templates
_brand.yml drives the web theme specifically (see Theming & Brand).

Render it: quarto render templates/my-poster/poster.qmd. Check poster.pdf for the printable version and poster.html for the web version.
Run the checks (optional, but worth it before you consider it done): Rscript scripts/render-all.R renders every template it finds and checks the output for known regressions. See Scripts & CI.
Regenerate the previews if you want updated images for your own README: Rscript scripts/make-previews.R (after re-rendering the PDFs).


3.1 Environment Requirements
To render a poster itself: Quarto (a version at or near the one pinned in .quarto-version) and R since every template’s R code chunks are part of the shipped example content, not the poster mechanism itself.

When you replace the demo analysis with your own R or Python code, only your own code’s package requirements apply.

As shipped, the three example posters use:

tidyverse, palmerpenguins, patchwork (all three templates)
broom (01-classic-academic only, for broom::tidy() model summaries)
knitr (all three, for knitr::kable() tables – normally auto-loaded by Quarto’s R engine, listed here for completeness)

No Python packages are required unless you add your own Python chunks.
No system libraries beyond a working R + Quarto install are needed for the print or web render themselves.

fonts (Source Sans 3, STIX Two Text) are fetched from Google and cached by Quarto at render time (see AGENTS.md’s “Fonts” section), not installed as system fonts.

To run the helper scripts in scripts/: all four use tidyverse and here.

make-previews.R additionally needs magick (Installing Magick, n.d.) (which needs the ImageMagick system library), and
check-column-balance.R needs pdftools (Jereon Ooms, n.d.) (which needs the poppler system library).
check-contrast.R needs only tidyverse/here – it’s pure source/CSS parsing, no rendering.

None of the scripts are required to render a poster; quarto render templates/<name>/poster.qmd alone is enough. - They exist to catch regressions (see Scripts & CI), and CI (.github/workflows/posters.yml) installs all of the above automatically via r-lib/actions/setup-r-dependencies, so you never need to install anything by hand just to see CI pass on a fork.
Is this an renv (Wickham and Ushey 2024) repo? No, deliberately not.

renv buys strict, pinned reproducibility of exact package versions, at the cost of a lockfile contributors must keep in sync and an renv::restore() step before anything runs.
For a small, stable package list on a repo meant to be forked and heavily edited by students building their own poster content (who will be adding whatever packages their analysis needs, not constrained by a lockfile), that friction outweighs the benefit here.
If you want tighter reproducibility for your own fork, e.g., pinning exact versions for a team where everyone must get identical output, renv::init() after cloning is a reasonable thing to layer on yourself; it just isn’t part of this template.

title: Why Typst?
text:
The print format here is poster-typst (Posit Software, PBC, n.d.), which typesets through Typst (“Overview - Typst Documentation,” n.d.) rather than through LaTeX (format: pdf).

Quarto’s Typst Basics guide (Allaire et al. 2024; J.J. Allaire et al. 2023) is the reference for everything in this section.

Why it fits posters well:

No TeX toolchain. Quarto ships the Typst CLI, so nothing beyond Quarto itself needs installing; no TinyTeX bootstrap, no per-package downloads on first render, no version drift between machines.

For a template repo other people are meant to clone and render, this is the single biggest practical win.

Fast, legible iteration. Typst is designed to be as capable as LaTeX while being easier to learn, and it renders quickly, which matters here, because tuning a poster is a loop of “render, look at the whole page, adjust a size, render again.”
Arbitrary page geometry is a first-class option. size: "48x36" (or "24x52") is just a format option; multi-column flow is num-columns. Getting the same from LaTeX means tikzposter/beamerposter plus a class-specific idiom for every layout decision.
Escape hatches that read like code. The few things Markdown can’t express are written as raw ```{=typst} blocks: #colbreak() to force a column, and #place(bottom + right, scope: "parent", float: true) to pin the Ethics panel to the physical page corner from inside a column.

Both are a couple of legible lines.
See Raw Typst and the Typst tutorial.

Inspectable intermediate. --metadata keep-typ=true preserves the generated .typ, which is how the dropped-acknowledgments bug in Notes / gotchas was actually diagnosed: the content was missing from the .typ, which located the fault in the Markdown, not in Typst.

What it costs, honestly:

A younger ecosystem. The vendored extension needed three local patches (see Notes / gotchas) for things a mature LaTeX poster class would already handle.

Quarto’s own Known Limitations (Posit Software, PBC, n.d.) note that default image sizing may not match other formats, which is exactly the out-width surprise documented in Templates.

Raw blocks are format-locked. A ```{=typst} block is invisible to HTML and vice versa, so genuinely dual-format content (the Ethics panel, the headline stat) has to be written twice and kept in sync by hand.
Different figure and citation defaults. Typst output defaults to fig-format: svg (these templates override it to png, see Notes / gotchas) and uses Typst’s own bibliography engine rather than Pandoc’s citeproc, which is why suppressing its automatic “Bibliography” heading needed a template partial.
LaTeX is still the right call if you need a specific journal/venue LaTeX class, heavy LaTeX-only math or TikZ, or a collaborator’s existing .tex workflow.

title: Scripts & CI
text:
scripts/ holds four R helpers, plus a shared registry they all read. All are optional, a plain quarto render still works.

Paths are resolved with the here package rather than requiring you to run from a specific working directory, and the template registry (scripts/templates.R) auto-discovers posters: either the multi-template layout shipped here (templates/<dir>/*.qmd, one per subdirectory), or, if you deleted templates/ and kept a single poster at the project’s top level under any filename, that one file instead.




Script
What it does




render-all.R
Renders every discovered template to both formats, then runs every check below (including delegating to check-contrast.R); one command for the whole suite. Exits non-zero on failure, so it can be wired into CI or a pre-commit hook. Pass --no-render to check existing output without re-rendering.


check-column-balance.R
Measures how far down each Typst column the content actually reaches. Usable standalone: Rscript scripts/check-column-balance.R templates/<name>/poster.pdf <num-columns>.


make-previews.R
Regenerates images/previews/preview-*.png and comparison.png from the rendered PDFs.


check-contrast.R
Audits every foreground/background pair in the output against WCAG AA and AAA. Parses the palette, the stylesheets’ own color:/background: rules (including both linear-gradient() stops), and each template’s print footer YAML, so a re-color is re-audited rather than checked against a stale copy. Fails below AA, or below AAA with --require-aaa. See Re-coloring the templates.



scripts/templates.R is the shared registry of templates (column counts, print sizes, expected column-fill baselines) that the other three read, so adding a template to the multi-template layout is a one-line edit there; a template discovered outside that registry (e.g. a renamed single-poster fork) just runs without a column-balance baseline to compare against.
A Makefile (OSDev, n.d.) wraps the common commands:
make render       # clear the stale Typst package cache, then render + check everything
make check        # run the checks against whatever output already exists (no render)
make clean-cache  # just clear .quarto/typst/packages (see the caching note below)
Every check in render-all.R exists because that failure actually happened once during development and was invisible in the render log:

pages: a content edit overflowing onto a second Typst page; a poster must be exactly one page.
divider: the web section divider disappearing from the HTML.
acknowledgments: the raw-HTML-in-a-conditional-div bug described under Notes / gotchas, which dropped the acknowledgments, grant number, and References heading from print while the web version looked perfect.
ethics: the Ethics & Broader Impact panel missing from either format (it is written once per format, so it can go missing from one).
balance: a column emptying out relative to its measured baseline.
#### after show rule: a #### heading placed above the level-3 show rule described under Notes / gotchas. Typst show rules only affect what follows them, so such a heading silently keeps the package’s “1) Heading:” run-in style.
contrast: a palette edit dropping a color below WCAG AA, delegated to check-contrast.R so the same audit stays usable on its own.



.github/workflows/posters.yml runs these same scripts on push and pull request via GitHub Actions (GitHub 2024), in three jobs (a workflow-authoring reference like (GitHub Actions Setup — Github_actions 2026), written for R packages specifically, is a useful pattern library even though this repo hand-writes its own YAML rather than generating it):








Job
Runs
Why




changes
A dorny/paths-filter check against the diff — no R, no Quarto
Cheap pre-check so the two jobs below only pay for a full R/Quarto toolchain install when their own inputs actually changed. Skipped only for a manual workflow_dispatch run, since there’s no diff to filter on.


contrast
check-contrast.R --require-aaa
Pure source parsing, no Quarto, no fonts, no rendering, so it is quick and its verdict is unambiguous. Every pair currently reaches AAA, so the strict gate is the meaningful one. Runs only when changes reports a color-relevant path touched (_brand.yml, scss/**, a template’s poster.qmd/*.scss, scripts/templates.R, scripts/check-contrast.R, or the vendored extension), or on manual dispatch.


render
render-all.R (both formats for all three templates, plus every output check)
Needs the Typst toolchain and system libraries for pdftools/magick, which are the fragile parts. Keeping it apart from contrast means a toolchain or font problem is never mistaken for an accessibility regression. Runs only when changes reports a render-relevant path touched (templates/**, scripts/**, _extensions/**, scss/**, _brand.yml, _quarto.yml, .quarto-version, or the workflow file itself), or on manual dispatch.



Both gates exist because a push touching none of those paths — a docs-only or README-only commit, say — previously still paid for the full job’s R/Quarto toolchain install regardless of relevance: 30-40 minutes observed for contrast alone, almost all of it a from-source tidyverse install with no cache, for an audit whose own logic runs in seconds. A job skipped this way reports as skipped rather than failing, which GitHub’s required-status-check logic treats as passing, so this is safe to use even where these jobs are required checks on main.
See AGENTS.md — an orientation file following the open AGENTS.md convention (Agentsmd/Agents.md 2026) for AI coding agents (and humans) working in a repo — for project orientation, the vendored extension’s local patches, and the open fonts issue.
Two caveats worth knowing before you rely on it:

Quarto’s release version matters. Both workflows pin quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2 to a specific Quarto version rather than tracking release; an unpinned run once picked up a pandoc/Typst-writer change that broke the institution-logo path substitution.

The version lives in one file, .quarto-version, which each workflow reads into a step output before calling setup@v2.
This way posters.yml and docs.yml cannot drift out of sync with each other the way two hardcoded copies could.
See Updating the pinned Quarto version below for the bump procedure, and why the pin stays even though the specific bug it was protecting against is now also patched at the source.

Fonts change layout, and layout is measured. poster.typ asks for STIX Two Text, and Quarto injects a Source Sans 3 show rule for headings; both are now declared as brand font resources in _brand.yml (source: google).

Quarto fetches and caches them under .quarto/typst/fonts/ at render time.
The GitHub runner needs no system fonts for the print render, and CI and local renders resolve the same faces by construction.
This is purely about print/CI reproducibility; see Theming & Brand for what the same _brand.yml declaration does – and doesn’t – deliver for the html output.




Bump .quarto-version deliberately rather than letting either workflow drift to a new release silently:

Install the candidate Quarto release locally.
Run make check-quarto-version to confirm quarto --version matches the release you just installed (it fails loudly on a mismatch, so you know you are about to test the version you think you are).
Run make render (renders every template and all output checks) and, if you touched docs-src/, quarto render docs-src too. Inspect the rendered PDFs/HTML, not just the check output – the balance/contrast checks catch some regressions, not all of them.
Only once that looks right, edit .quarto-version and commit. Both posters.yml and docs.yml read the same file, so one edit updates both workflows.

Why the pin stays, even after the path fix. _extensions/quarto-ext/poster/typst-show.typ now strips a stray leading backslash from the substituted institution-logo path defensively (see Notes / gotchas), which patches the specific bug that originally motivated pinning.

That is not a reason to switch either workflow back to tracking release: the pin’s job is to make a render on a given commit reproducible run to run, and it was already carrying that weight for other reasons before this bug was ever found, e.g.. the font-resolution differences discussed in AGENTS.md.
A future pandoc/Typst-writer change breaking something else entirely (a different substitution, color handling, heading numbering) would be just as invisible under release as this one was, and there is no way to defensively patch a bug that hasn’t happened yet.
Tracking release trades a small, bounded maintenance cost (the four steps above, only needed when you actually want a newer Quarto) for an unbounded and unpredictable one (CI failing on an unrelated commit because GitHub’s runner picked up a new Quarto release overnight).

This documentation site itself is a separate, nested Quarto website project: sources live in docs-src/ (its own docs-src/_quarto.yml), rendering to docs/. GitHub Pages (Settings -> Pages: branch main, /docs) serves that committed docs/ folder directly; there’s no publish step in CI;

.github/workflows/docs.yml renders docs-src/ fresh and then diffs the result against the committed docs/, independent of the two jobs above.
If they differ, someone edited docs-src/ (or an image copy-images.sh pulls in) without re-rendering, a stale /docs is otherwise invisible in a PR diff, since docs-src/*.qmd changes review fine on their own.
After editing anything under docs-src/, re-render and commit the result: quarto render docs-src.







NoteThis is a simplified Pages setup, on purpose



The pattern here, render locally, commit the rendered docs/ folder, point GitHub Pages (Settings → Pages: branch main, /docs) at it directly, is not the only way to publish a Quarto site to GitHub Pages, and it is not what most production projects do.

It was chosen deliberately for this repo because it needs no GitHub Actions permissions, no deploy step, and no separate gh-pages branch to reason about: what’s on main in docs/ is exactly what’s live, and any contributor can quarto render docs-src locally and see precisely what will publish before pushing.

The trade-off is real, and worth knowing before copying this into your own repo:

Rendered HTML/CSS/JS lives in git history like any other tracked file, so PR diffs touching docs-src/ also carry a (usually large, machine-generated) diff of docs/.
Nothing enforces that docs/ actually matches docs-src/ at any given commit except a CI job (.github/workflows/docs.yml) that re-renders and diffs the two after the fact — it catches a forgotten re-render, but only after the commit is already up.
output-dir: ../docs pointing outside docs-src/’s own project directory is why quarto render docs-src prints the harmless-but-odd site_libs/“unexpected path configuration” warnings documented in AGENTS.md — an artifact of this specific layout, not a sign of anything broken.

When this simplified approach is a reasonable fit: a small site with one or a handful of maintainers, low-frequency publishing, and a preference for “no CI, no Actions permissions to configure, nothing to debug beyond a normal git commit.” That describes this repo.
When to reach instead for a proper build-and-deploy workflow (render to an ignored, in-project output directory like _site, then publish via actions/deploy-pages or quarto publish gh-pages, with GitHub Pages set to source from “GitHub Actions” rather than a branch): a site with many contributors, frequent changes, or a desire to keep generated files out of git entirely.

That is the more standard, more scalable pattern, and the one worth learning if you are setting up Pages for a repo of your own from scratch.

make render       # clear the stale Typst package cache, then render + check everything
make check        # run the checks against whatever output already exists (no render)
make clean-cache  # just clear .quarto/typst/packages (see the caching note below)
Every check in render-all.R exists because that failure actually happened once during development and was invisible in the render log:

pages: a content edit overflowing onto a second Typst page; a poster must be exactly one page.
divider: the web section divider disappearing from the HTML.
acknowledgments: the raw-HTML-in-a-conditional-div bug described under Notes / gotchas, which dropped the acknowledgments, grant number, and References heading from print while the web version looked perfect.
ethics: the Ethics & Broader Impact panel missing from either format (it is written once per format, so it can go missing from one).
balance: a column emptying out relative to its measured baseline.
#### after show rule: a #### heading placed above the level-3 show rule described under Notes / gotchas. Typst show rules only affect what follows them, so such a heading silently keeps the package’s “1) Heading:” run-in style.
contrast: a palette edit dropping a color below WCAG AA, delegated to check-contrast.R so the same audit stays usable on its own.



.github/workflows/posters.yml runs these same scripts on push and pull request via GitHub Actions (GitHub 2024), in three jobs (a workflow-authoring reference like (GitHub Actions Setup — Github_actions 2026), written for R packages specifically, is a useful pattern library even though this repo hand-writes its own YAML rather than generating it):








Job
Runs
Why




changes
A dorny/paths-filter check against the diff — no R, no Quarto
Cheap pre-check so the two jobs below only pay for a full R/Quarto toolchain install when their own inputs actually changed. Skipped only for a manual workflow_dispatch run, since there’s no diff to filter on.


contrast
check-contrast.R --require-aaa
Pure source parsing, no Quarto, no fonts, no rendering, so it is quick and its verdict is unambiguous. Every pair currently reaches AAA, so the strict gate is the meaningful one. Runs only when changes reports a color-relevant path touched (_brand.yml, scss/**, a template’s poster.qmd/*.scss, scripts/templates.R, scripts/check-contrast.R, or the vendored extension), or on manual dispatch.


render
render-all.R (both formats for all three templates, plus every output check)
Needs the Typst toolchain and system libraries for pdftools/magick, which are the fragile parts. Keeping it apart from contrast means a toolchain or font problem is never mistaken for an accessibility regression. Runs only when changes reports a render-relevant path touched (templates/**, scripts/**, _extensions/**, scss/**, _brand.yml, _quarto.yml, .quarto-version, or the workflow file itself), or on manual dispatch.



Both gates exist because a push touching none of those paths — a docs-only or README-only commit, say — previously still paid for the full job’s R/Quarto toolchain install regardless of relevance: 30-40 minutes observed for contrast alone, almost all of it a from-source tidyverse install with no cache, for an audit whose own logic runs in seconds. A job skipped this way reports as skipped rather than failing, which GitHub’s required-status-check logic treats as passing, so this is safe to use even where these jobs are required checks on main.
See AGENTS.md — an orientation file following the open AGENTS.md convention (Agentsmd/Agents.md 2026) for AI coding agents (and humans) working in a repo — for project orientation, the vendored extension’s local patches, and the open fonts issue.
Two caveats worth knowing before you rely on it:

Quarto’s release version matters. Both workflows pin quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2 to a specific Quarto version rather than tracking release; an unpinned run once picked up a pandoc/Typst-writer change that broke the institution-logo path substitution.

The version lives in one file, .quarto-version, which each workflow reads into a step output before calling setup@v2.
This way posters.yml and docs.yml cannot drift out of sync with each other the way two hardcoded copies could.
See Updating the pinned Quarto version below for the bump procedure, and why the pin stays even though the specific bug it was protecting against is now also patched at the source.

Fonts change layout, and layout is measured. poster.typ asks for STIX Two Text, and Quarto injects a Source Sans 3 show rule for headings; both are now declared as brand font resources in _brand.yml (source: google).

Quarto fetches and caches them under .quarto/typst/fonts/ at render time.
The GitHub runner needs no system fonts for the print render, and CI and local renders resolve the same faces by construction.
This is purely about print/CI reproducibility; see Theming & Brand for what the same _brand.yml declaration does – and doesn’t – deliver for the html output.




Bump .quarto-version deliberately rather than letting either workflow drift to a new release silently:

Install the candidate Quarto release locally.
Run make check-quarto-version to confirm quarto --version matches the release you just installed (it fails loudly on a mismatch, so you know you are about to test the version you think you are).
Run make render (renders every template and all output checks) and, if you touched docs-src/, quarto render docs-src too. Inspect the rendered PDFs/HTML, not just the check output – the balance/contrast checks catch some regressions, not all of them.
Only once that looks right, edit .quarto-version and commit. Both posters.yml and docs.yml read the same file, so one edit updates both workflows.

Why the pin stays, even after the path fix. _extensions/quarto-ext/poster/typst-show.typ now strips a stray leading backslash from the substituted institution-logo path defensively (see Notes / gotchas), which patches the specific bug that originally motivated pinning.

That is not a reason to switch either workflow back to tracking release: the pin’s job is to make a render on a given commit reproducible run to run, and it was already carrying that weight for other reasons before this bug was ever found, e.g.. the font-resolution differences discussed in AGENTS.md.
A future pandoc/Typst-writer change breaking something else entirely (a different substitution, color handling, heading numbering) would be just as invisible under release as this one was, and there is no way to defensively patch a bug that hasn’t happened yet.
Tracking release trades a small, bounded maintenance cost (the four steps above, only needed when you actually want a newer Quarto) for an unbounded and unpredictable one (CI failing on an unrelated commit because GitHub’s runner picked up a new Quarto release overnight).

This documentation site itself is a separate, nested Quarto website project: sources live in docs-src/ (its own docs-src/_quarto.yml), rendering to docs/. GitHub Pages (Settings -> Pages: branch main, /docs) serves that committed docs/ folder directly; there’s no publish step in CI;

.github/workflows/docs.yml renders docs-src/ fresh and then diffs the result against the committed docs/, independent of the two jobs above.
If they differ, someone edited docs-src/ (or an image copy-images.sh pulls in) without re-rendering, a stale /docs is otherwise invisible in a PR diff, since docs-src/*.qmd changes review fine on their own.
After editing anything under docs-src/, re-render and commit the result: quarto render docs-src.







NoteThis is a simplified Pages setup, on purpose



The pattern here, render locally, commit the rendered docs/ folder, point GitHub Pages (Settings → Pages: branch main, /docs) at it directly, is not the only way to publish a Quarto site to GitHub Pages, and it is not what most production projects do.

It was chosen deliberately for this repo because it needs no GitHub Actions permissions, no deploy step, and no separate gh-pages branch to reason about: what’s on main in docs/ is exactly what’s live, and any contributor can quarto render docs-src locally and see precisely what will publish before pushing.

The trade-off is real, and worth knowing before copying this into your own repo:

Rendered HTML/CSS/JS lives in git history like any other tracked file, so PR diffs touching docs-src/ also carry a (usually large, machine-generated) diff of docs/.
Nothing enforces that docs/ actually matches docs-src/ at any given commit except a CI job (.github/workflows/docs.yml) that re-renders and diffs the two after the fact — it catches a forgotten re-render, but only after the commit is already up.
output-dir: ../docs pointing outside docs-src/’s own project directory is why quarto render docs-src prints the harmless-but-odd site_libs/“unexpected path configuration” warnings documented in AGENTS.md — an artifact of this specific layout, not a sign of anything broken.

When this simplified approach is a reasonable fit: a small site with one or a handful of maintainers, low-frequency publishing, and a preference for “no CI, no Actions permissions to configure, nothing to debug beyond a normal git commit.” That describes this repo.
When to reach instead for a proper build-and-deploy workflow (render to an ignored, in-project output directory like _site, then publish via actions/deploy-pages or quarto publish gh-pages, with GitHub Pages set to source from “GitHub Actions” rather than a branch): a site with many contributors, frequent changes, or a desire to keep generated files out of git entirely.

That is the more standard, more scalable pattern, and the one worth learning if you are setting up Pages for a repo of your own from scratch.

2 Forking vs. cloning: what runs, and how to control it
This repo ships two GitHub Actions workflows (posters.yml, docs.yml). What happens to them depends on how you got your own copy of the repo, and that trips people up often enough to spell out explicitly.

2.1 Forking (clicking GitHub’s “Fork” button)
GitHub copies the workflow files into your fork, but leaves Actions disabled on the fork by default. This is a deliberate, blanket security measure for every fork of a public repo, not specific to this one.

The first time you open your fork’s Actions tab, GitHub shows a banner (“Workflows aren’t being run on this fork”) with a button, “I understand my workflows, go ahead and enable them.”

Nothing runs, not a push, not a manual trigger, until you click it (or do the CLI equivalent below).
Once enabled, pushes to your fork’s branches trigger posters.yml/docs.yml exactly as they do here, using your fork’s own Actions minutes.

Opening a pull request from your fork back to this repo is different again.

That pull_request event runs under this repo’s Actions settings (already enabled), not your fork’s, but with two restrictions that apply to any fork’s PR, regardless of whether you enabled Actions on your fork:
The GITHUB_TOKEN the workflow gets is read-only and has no access to this repo’s secrets.
By default, a first-time contributor’s workflow run requires a maintainer to click Approve and run in the Actions tab before it executes at all.
Every run after your first merged contribution runs automatically.




2.2 Cloning (git clone + push to your own new repository, not a GitHub fork)

If you git clone this repo and push its history to a brand-new repository you created yourself (rather than using GitHub’s “Fork” button), none of the fork-specific restrictions above apply. — GitHub has no record that your repository descends from this one.
Actions are enabled by default on a new repository, the same as any other repo you create, subject only to your own account’s or organization’s Actions policy (Settings → Actions → General).
Your first push already triggers posters.yml/docs.yml, with no opt-in banner to click.
A plain local git clone with no push anywhere never triggers anything — workflow runs are a server-side GitHub event, not something git clone or a local quarto render can cause on its own.



2.3 Enabling/disabling from the command line
All of the following use the gh CLI and require admin access to the repository in question (your fork, or your own clone-turned-repo).
Permanently enable or disable Actions for the whole repository is the CLI equivalent of the fork’s “enable workflows” banner, or of Settings → Actions → General → Actions permissions:
gh api -X PUT repos/OWNER/REPO/actions/permissions -f enabled=true   # or false
Permanently enable or disable one specific workflow (leaves the rest, and the repo-wide switch above, untouched):
gh workflow disable posters.yml   # stops it from running or being manually triggered
gh workflow enable posters.yml    # re-enables it
Run a workflow exactly once, without changing either persistent switch above. Both posters.yml and docs.yml declare workflow_dispatch as a trigger already, so a single on-demand run (Actions enabled, this workflow not disabled) is:
gh workflow run posters.yml --ref main
This queues one run of the current main (or whatever --ref you give it) and leaves the workflow’s enabled/disabled state exactly as it was before and after, unlike gh workflow disable/enable, which persist until you change them again.

3 Notes / gotchas
The vendored _extensions/quarto-ext/poster has local patches. If you re-install/update the extension, re-apply all of them:

poster.typ accepts the institution logo as already-loaded Typst content (loaded once in typst-show.typ) rather than a bare path string, because Typst packages cannot read files outside their own package directory (see the _univ_logo_img handling in typst-show.typ).
poster.typ / typst-show.typ add a footer-text-color format option (defaults to white) so the footer text stays legible against dark footer-color values. Set it to a dark color if you pick a light footer background (see 01-classic-academic’s footer-text-color: "25406A").
biblio.typ (a new template-partial, registered in _extension.yml) sets title: none on the generated #bibliography(...) call, so Typst’s own default “Bibliography” heading doesn’t duplicate each template’s own #### References heading.
poster.typ also scales the footer’s font sizes down (never up) on posters narrower than the extension’s documented 36in default, so the footer row (URL + text + emails, packed with h(1fr) spacers) doesn’t wrap outside its colored background block on narrower prints like 03-minimal-story’s 24in width.
typst-show.typ strips a stray leading backslash from the substituted institution-logo path before calling image() on it, defending against a pandoc/Typst-writer bug that once inserted one and broke the render with “path must not contain a backslash” (see Updating the pinned Quarto version).

It is a no-op when the path is already clean, so it is safe regardless of Quarto version.
Because Quarto caches the vendored local Typst package under each project’s .quarto/typst/packages/local/typst-poster/, edits to poster.typ only take effect after that cached copy is refreshed (delete .quarto/ or copy the updated file over it, or just run make render). A plain quarto render will silently keep using the stale cached version.

Every template’s poster-typst format sets fig-format: png. Without it, Typst’s default (fig-format: svg) asks R’s Cairo graphics device to render each plot, which can fail with a missing X11/Cairo shared-library error on machines without XQuartz (common on Apple Silicon macOS, and on Linux without libcairo2-dev).

Installing XQuartz/libcairo dev packages fixes it at the source; fig-format: png sidesteps it by using R’s built-in PNG device instead, at a small cost in image sharpness for print.

Never put a raw <hr> (or other raw HTML) inside a ::: {.content-visible when-format="html"} div. Doing so silently discards every element after it in the Typst output – the templates lost their section divider, the entire Acknowledgments block (advisor, grant number, code/data link), and the #### References heading from the printed PDF, while still rendering fine on the web. Use a ```{=html} raw block instead, which HTML picks up and Typst ignores cleanly.
Column balance: the shipped samples do not fill their columns evenly, and that is accepted slack rather than a bug – 02-modern-cards reaches ~44% down column 1 vs ~82% down column 2, and 03-minimal-story ends ~79% down its single column. The Evidence figure is one ~10in-tall indivisible block, so moving 02’s #colbreak() past it only inverts the gap (measured 91%/29%, a wider spread). Real content is the remedy. Baselines live in scripts/templates.R; render-all.R fails on a drop of more than 10 points from them.
Web banner contrast: the title banner is a gradient, so banner text must clear its lighter stop, not just the dark one.

The original $au-light-blue author/date color measured 6.97:1 on navy but only 3.59:1 on the $au-blue stop, a WCAG AA failure.
All banner text is now plain white on a darkened light stop ($au-blue-banner, 7.21:1), and link and grey body text were darkened to clear AAA too.
See Re-coloring the templates, and run Rscript scripts/check-contrast.R after any color change.

#### headings arrive as Typst level 3, not level 4. Quarto maps markdown ## to =, shifting every heading up one level, so the closing-matter headings land on the poster package’s level-3 style: a numbered, italic, colon-terminated run-in that prints as “1) Acknowledgments:” and reads like a numbered list item.

Each template overrides this with a #show heading.where(level: 3) rule in the raw Typst block just above #### Acknowledgments, defined after the package’s own show heading rule so it takes precedence.
A #### heading placed earlier in the poster still gets the package’s run-in style, since Typst show rules only apply to content after them.

Font-size hierarchy is not automatic. The poster package defaults title-font-size to 48pt and authors-font-size to 36pt, and derives level-1 headings as body-font-size + 16.

If you shrink title-font-size to fit a long title (as 03-minimal-story needs to at 24in wide), lower authors-font-size too and keep the title above body-font-size + 16, or the author line and section headings will print larger than the title.

.quarto/, rendered *.pdf/*.typ/poster.html, and *_files/ directories are gitignored as build output.
